stages.title: Pathology fundamentals
stages.hook: Two patients cut a finger. One heals in a week, the other develops a spreading red, hot, swollen wound. What is going on inside the tissue?
explain: Pathology is the study of disease: its causes (aetiology), how it develops (pathogenesis), the changes it produces in cells and tissues, and the effects on function. Main causes include infection, inflammation and immune disorders, injury, poor blood supply (ischaemia), genetic disease, abnormal growth (neoplasia), metabolic problems, and degeneration.

Inflammation is the body's response to injury or infection. Its classic signs are redness, heat, swelling and pain, and loss of function. Blood vessels widen and leak, and white cells arrive. Acute inflammation is rapid and usually helpful; chronic inflammation is long-lasting and can damage tissue.

Cells respond to stress by adapting (growing bigger or smaller), becoming injured (reversibly or irreversibly) or dying. Ischaemia, a lack of blood supply, injures cells fast because they run out of oxygen. A neoplasm is an abnormal growth. Benign ones stay local; malignant ones invade nearby tissue and can spread (metastasise) to other organs.

example.q: A fictional finger wound is red, hot, swollen and painful 2 days after injury. Which process explains this?
steps: Redness and heat: blood vessels widen, bringing more blood.
Swelling: vessels leak fluid and cells into the tissue.
Pain: chemicals released irritate nerve endings. These are the classic signs of acute inflammation.

analogies.city: After a fire, emergency crews rush in, roads fill and the area is busy. Inflammation is that emergency response.
analogies.home: A burst pipe floods a room. Repair crews and cleaners arrive, but if the leak is ignored the damage grows.
analogies.nature: A forest after a storm: fast clean-up and regrowth, but fires that smoulder can destroy it.
analogies.tech: A system alert triggers repair processes; constant false alarms exhaust the system, like chronic inflammation.

stages.mnemonic: Rubor, calor, tumor, dolor: red, hot, swollen, painful (plus loss of function).
terms: The cause or causes of a disease.
How a disease develops step by step.
Too little blood supply to a tissue.
Spread of a cancer from its origin to other parts of the body.
An abnormal growth of cells, which may be benign or malignant.

misc.right: Acute inflammation is a helpful defence and repair response. Harm arises when it is excessive, in the wrong place or chronic.

stages.limits: Disease mechanisms are far more complex than this overview, and many diseases combine several causes.

trip.prompt: Find the five cardinal signs of inflammation and a cause of each.

questions.why: It examines causes and changes of disease.

To cool the whole body down only
To store fat in the area
To make new bone at the site

o: Malignant

Order the basic steps of acute inflammation.
questions.why: Acute inflammation is a sequence from trigger to repair.

o: Possible chronic inflammation needing assessment
A healthy joint with normal wear
Acute healing that will soon finish
A normal sign of ageing in every case
questions.why: Long-lasting inflammation can damage joints and needs a cause found.

questions.q: Why does a blocked artery injure cells so quickly?
o: Cells need a constant oxygen supply
Arteries hold large stores of fat
Cells dislike the presence of blood
Blocked arteries cool the whole body at once
questions.why: Without oxygen cells cannot make energy.

questions.q: Explain why acute inflammation is useful but chronic inflammation can be harmful.
questions.model: Acute inflammation brings defence cells and starts repair, then settles. If it persists, the ongoing response damages normal tissue and can cause scarring and disease.
questions.why: Duration and control determine whether inflammation helps or harms.

Certainly malignant
An infection
Normal tissue

o: Adaptation by shrinking (atrophy)
Cancer starting inside the shrunken tissue
Immediate death of every cell
Inflammation from an infection
panel.why: Cells shrink when workload or stimulation falls.

panel.q: Why do clinicians look for the cause (aetiology), not just treat the symptom?
panel.model: Treating only a symptom can mask the problem and let the cause worsen, whereas finding the underlying cause lets treatment be effective and prevents recurrence.

teach.model: Pathology studies disease: its causes and the changes in cells and tissues. Inflammation is the body's response to injury, with redness, heat, swelling and pain. Malignant growths invade and spread; benign ones stay local.

points.ask: What is the difference between benign and malignant?

stages.title: Pharmacology and medication safety
stages.hook: A medicine can save a life or cause harm, depending on who takes it and how. What should every clinician check first?
explain: Pharmacology studies how drugs act. Two key ideas: pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion) and pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body. The liver often breaks drugs down and the kidneys often remove them, so liver or kidney disease can change how much drug stays in the body.

Every medicine has benefits and risks. Side effects are unwanted effects. An adverse reaction is a harmful response, and an allergy is an immune reaction that can range from rash to life-threatening anaphylaxis. Drug interactions happen when one medicine changes the effect of another. Some medicines have a narrow therapeutic window, meaning the gap between helpful and harmful amounts is small.

Medication safety checks (often called the rights): right patient, right drug, right route, right time, right reason, with allergy status and other medicines checked. Look-alike and sound-alike names, handwriting, and busy interruptions cause errors. Report errors and near-misses so systems can improve. Prescribing is done by authorised clinicians following guidelines. This game never gives doses.

example.q: A fictional patient with kidney disease is to start a medicine mostly cleared by the kidneys. What should the junior do?
steps: Recognise the drug is removed by the kidneys.
Poor kidney function means the drug may build up.
Check with the senior doctor and pharmacist before prescribing; do not guess.
example.a: Check with a senior and pharmacist because the drug may build up

analogies.home: A bath tap and drain: if the drain (kidney) is slow, water (drug) builds up.
analogies.city: A road network with a toll: some drugs need the right route and time to arrive safely.
analogies.farm: A vet adjusts treatment to the animal's size and health.
analogies.tech: Software updates can clash with other apps, like drug interactions.

stages.mnemonic: Right patient, drug, route, time, reason, and Allergies Checked.
terms: What the body does to a drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion.
What a drug does to the body.
A harmful, unintended response to a medicine.
When one drug changes how another acts.
The range between a helpful effect and a harmful one.

misc.wrong: Natural or herbal products are always safe.
misc.right: Herbal products are drugs too. They can have side effects and interact with prescribed medicines.

stages.limits: This game deals with ideas only and gives no doses or regimens. Real prescribing follows local guidelines and an authorised prescriber.

questions.why: Little room between benefit and harm.

questions.why: Checking prevents errors; speaking up is a safety skill.

Why should a clinician ask about herbal and over-the-counter products as well as prescriptions?
questions.model: Herbal and over-the-counter products can interact with prescribed medicines or cause side effects, so a full list keeps prescribing safe.

panel.q: A junior doctor realises they have prescribed the wrong medicine, but it has not been given. What is best?
o: Correct it, tell the team and report the near-miss

panel.why: A just culture learns from near-misses.

panel.q: An older patient takes many medicines. Why does a review help?
o: Interactions and side effects may add up

panel.q: Why is it sensible that dose and choice of medicine be decided by a trained prescriber rather than guessed?
panel.model: Safe prescribing depends on the patient's age, size, organ function and other medicines, and wrong amounts can cause harm, so trained prescribers use guidelines.

teach.model: Medicines have benefits and risks. The body absorbs, spreads, breaks down and removes them, and the liver and kidneys matter. Always check the right patient, drug, route and time, and look for allergies and interactions.

points.ask: How does the body handle a drug?

stages.title: Clinical reasoning
stages.hook: Two doctors see the same patient. One jumps to the first idea, the other keeps an open mind. Which one catches a rare danger?
explain: Clinical reasoning is the thinking that turns a patient's story, examination and tests into a diagnosis and plan. Experienced clinicians often use pattern recognition (fast, intuitive, System 1 thinking). When the case is unusual or risky, they slow down and use analytical (System 2) reasoning.

A common method is hypothetico-deductive: gather a few clues, form a short list of possible causes, then choose questions and tests that best tell them apart, updating the list with each new clue. Think in probabilities: common things are common, but always ask 'what dangerous condition must I not miss?'

Cognitive biases cause errors. Anchoring is sticking to the first idea. Confirmation bias is seeking only evidence that supports your idea. Premature closure is stopping the search too early. Reflection, second opinions and checklists reduce bias. Being willing to say 'I might be wrong' and escalating to a senior is a strength.

example.q: A fictional patient with a headache is assumed to have tension headache. A new clue appears: sudden onset, 'worst ever', with neck stiffness. What should the clinician do?
steps: The new clues do not fit the first idea (anchoring risk).
Sudden severe headache with neck stiffness is a red flag for serious causes such as bleeding around the brain or meningitis.
Re-open the list, treat as urgent and escalate.
example.a: Revise the diagnosis, treat as urgent and escalate

analogies.home: A detective keeps several suspects until the evidence narrows them.
analogies.sport: A coach changes tactics when the first plan fails.
analogies.tech: A technician starts with common faults but checks serious ones.
analogies.sea: A navigator corrects the course when new readings arrive.

stages.mnemonic: Common first, dangerous never missed; keep re-checking.
terms: Thinking that links information to diagnosis and plan.
Sticking to an early idea despite new evidence.
Looking only for facts that support your idea.
Stopping the search once a diagnosis seems found.

misc.wrong: Good doctors know the answer instantly.
misc.right: Good doctors reason carefully, stay open to other possibilities and ask for help.

trip.prompt: Find the list of cognitive biases in diagnosis and match one to a story.

A treatment given on a ship
Using an anchor weight in surgery
A laboratory test for infection
questions.why: It blocks updating with new evidence.

questions.q: Confirmation bias means...
o: Seeking only evidence that supports your idea
Confirming a hospital booking well in advance
Checking a drug dose twice before giving it
Always trusting the most senior person
questions.why: It ignores evidence against your idea.

questions.q: Which approach helps reduce bias?
o: Pausing to reconsider and asking for a second opinion
Deciding faster to save time
Ignoring odd findings that do not fit
Avoiding tests to keep the picture simple

items: Make a short list of possible causes
Choose questions or tests to separate them
Update the list with the results

Drop it from the list because it is rare
Ignore the story and rely on the test
Wait for it to become obvious before acting

questions.q: Match the bias to an example.
Fast pattern recognition is best when...
o: The case is typical and low risk
The case is unusual and dangerous
Information is missing
Nobody agrees
questions.why: Switch to slow analytic thinking when the case is atypical or risky.

questions.q: A fictional patient's test result does not fit the working diagnosis. What should the junior do?
o: Reconsider the diagnosis and discuss with a senior
Throw out the result as probably faulty
Ignore it and keep the working diagnosis
Repeat nothing and write the same plan

questions.q: Why use checklists in complex cases?
o: They help prevent missed steps under pressure
They are meant to replace thinking altogether
They slow patients down on the ward
They add new errors to the process

questions.q: Explain why saying 'I might be wrong' can improve patient safety.
questions.model: Admitting that you might be wrong keeps you open to new evidence and willing to ask for help, which reduces bias and missed diagnoses.

panel.q: A diagnosis has been written in the notes by a previous doctor. New evidence disagrees. What is the best approach?
o: Re-evaluate rather than accept the label
Trust the earlier label because a doctor wrote it
Delete the old notes and start again
Stop treating until someone else decides
panel.why: Diagnostic labels can carry forward errors.

panel.q: A very tired night-shift doctor feels sure about a diagnosis. What helps?
o: Pause, double-check and consider alternatives
Trust the strong feeling and act on it at once
Skip further tests to finish sooner
Never ask for help from a colleague

panel.q: Why is 'what must I not miss?' a useful question even when a benign cause is most likely?
panel.model: Even if a benign cause is most likely, missing a rare but dangerous cause can be disastrous, so it is actively excluded.
panel.why: Risk weighs more than probability alone.

teach.model: Clinical reasoning links the story, examination and tests to a diagnosis. Doctors make a short list of causes, test them and update. Biases like anchoring can mislead, so doctors stay open-minded and ask seniors.

points.ask: How do doctors work out a diagnosis?

stages.title: Differential diagnosis
stages.hook: A fictional patient has chest pain. Is it the heart, the lungs, the stomach, the muscles or the nerves? How do you sort the list?
explain: A differential diagnosis is a ranked list of conditions that could explain the patient's problem. It starts from the main symptom and the patient's age and risk factors, then uses clues from the history, examination and tests to move conditions up or down the list.
Rank by three things: how likely each is, how dangerous it is if missed, and how treatable it is. A dangerous condition stays on the list until it is reasonably excluded, even if it is less likely.

For chest pain, the differential includes heart attack, angina, pulmonary embolism (a clot in the lungs), pneumonia or pleurisy, pneumothorax, reflux, muscle strain, and anxiety. Features that support each differ. For example, pain that is sharp and worse on breathing in may point to the lining of the lung; pain on exertion that eases with rest suggests angina; tender chest wall suggests a muscular cause. Tests such as an ECG, blood tests and chest X-ray help separate causes.

example.q: A fictional 60-year-old with diabetes has crushing central chest pain with sweating for 30 minutes. How should the differential be ranked?
steps: Dangerous and likely: heart attack goes to the top.
Also dangerous: aortic problems and a clot in the lungs, so keep them listed.
Less dangerous causes such as reflux stay lower but are considered later.
example.a: Heart attack at the top, with other dangerous causes kept on the list; this is an emergency

analogies.home: When the lights go out, you check the fuse first, but you also check for fire.
analogies.tech: A support agent lists likely faults and checks the dangerous ones first.
analogies.farm: A vet considers common and serious causes for a lame animal.
analogies.city: Emergency control lists possible causes of a power cut and checks the most dangerous first.

stages.mnemonic: Likely, Lethal, Treatable: rank by three Ls.
terms: A ranked list of possible explanations for a patient's problem.
Something that raises the chance of a disease.
A blood clot blocking an artery in the lungs.
To make a diagnosis very unlikely using evidence.

misc.wrong: The differential is a list that must be fixed at the start.
misc.right: It changes as new information arrives.

stages.limits: Real differentials depend on age, sex, setting and local disease patterns, and are always shaped by clinical judgement.

o: Escalate to a senior immediately
Send home with advice to rest
Repeat the ECG in a week's time at clinic
Ignore it as probably old
questions.why: Possible heart attack is time critical.

questions.q: Why does a doctor keep a dangerous diagnosis on the list even if it is unlikely?
questions.model: Because missing a serious condition can cause great harm, it remains on the list until tests or the clinical picture reasonably exclude it, even if it is unlikely.

panel.q: A patient has several conditions at once. How does this affect the differential?
o: Symptoms can have more than one cause
There can only ever be one diagnosis
It makes the differential list shorter
It makes further tests unnecessary
panel.why: Hickam's dictum: patients can have many diseases.

panel.q: Give two features of a good differential diagnosis.
panel.model: It is ranked by likelihood and danger, includes serious causes that must not be missed, and is updated as new information arrives.
panel.why: Good lists are ranked and flexible.

teach.model: A differential diagnosis is a ranked list of possible causes. We rank by how likely each is and how dangerous it is, keep dangerous ones until excluded and update the list as we learn more.

points.ask: Does the list stay the same?

stages.title: Laboratory test interpretation
stages.hook: A test for a rare disease is 95 percent accurate, yet most people who test positive may not have it. How can that be?
explain: To interpret a result, compare it with the reference range, think about the patient's situation and look at the trend. Typical adult values used in this game: haemoglobin about 12 to 17 g/dL (varies by sex); white cell count about 4 to 11 × 10⁹ per litre; sodium 135 to 145 mmol/L; potassium 3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L; fasting glucose about 4 to 6 mmol/L.

Sensitivity = true positives ÷ all people with the disease. Specificity = true negatives ÷ all people without the disease. The predictive value of a positive test depends on how common the disease is (prevalence). When a disease is rare, even a good test gives many false positives compared with true positives.

Interpret in context: a low haemoglobin means anaemia, but the cause needs more tests. A high white cell count suggests infection or inflammation. A very high or low potassium can disturb the heart rhythm and is treated as urgent. Always check that the sample, the patient and the units are right.

example.q: A disease affects 1 in 1000 people. A test has 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity. Of 100,000 tested people, how many true positives and false positives?
steps: People with disease: 100,000 ÷ 1000 = 100. True positives: 99% of 100 = 99.
People without disease: 99,900. False positives: 1% of 99,900 = 999.
So positives are 99 true and 999 false: most positives are false.
example.a: 99 true positives and 999 false positives, so a positive test is mostly false when the disease is rare

analogies.home: A smoke alarm that goes off at toast often raises false alarms when fires are rare.
analogies.sport: A referee's offside call is accurate overall but still has errors on rare, tight cases.
analogies.tech: A spam filter flags some real mail when real spam is rare.
analogies.farm: A rain gauge is good at detecting storms but may read wrongly in drizzle.

stages.mnemonic: SnNout, SpPin: a Sensitive test, when Negative, rules OUT; a Specific test, when Positive, rules IN.
terms: Proportion of people with disease who test positive.
Proportion of people without disease who test negative.
How common a disease is in a population.
A positive result in someone who does not have the condition.

misc.wrong: A 95 percent accurate test means a positive result is 95 percent likely to be true.
misc.right: The chance that a positive is real depends on how common the disease is as well as the test's accuracy.

stages.limits: Reference ranges vary by laboratory, age, sex and method, and units differ between countries; always use the local range.

Normal for most adults
Too much oxygen carried in the blood
Dehydration only, needing no more tests

questions.q: A very rare disease is screened with a good test. Why do many positives turn out false?
o: Because the disease is rare, false positives outnumber true positives
The test is lying, so it should be dropped
Rare diseases cause the test itself to give false results
Positives are always wrong whatever the disease
questions.why: Low prevalence reduces the positive predictive value.

questions.q: Match the result to the first thought.
questions.why: Results guide next steps in context.

questions.q: Why should a single abnormal result be repeated or interpreted with the clinical picture?
questions.model: Results can be affected by sample or lab error and normal variation, so doctors repeat them or interpret them with the patient's condition and trend.

panel.q: A screening test with 99% specificity is used on 10,000 healthy people. About how many false positives?
o: About 100
About 1
About 9,900
About 10

panel.q: A result looks impossible, such as a potassium of 9 in a well person. What is the best first step?
o: Suspect a sample or lab problem and repeat, while assessing the patient
Treat as true immediately without thinking
Ignore it because it looks unusual
Delete the report from the record
panel.why: Haemolysed samples can falsely raise potassium, but do not ignore risk.

panel.q: Explain why the same positive test can mean different things in a high-risk and a low-risk person.
panel.model: In a high-risk group the disease is common, so a positive is more likely to be true; in a low-risk group the disease is rare, so more positives are false.

teach.model: A result is compared with a reference range and the patient's story. Sensitivity shows how many people with disease are found, and specificity shows how many without disease are correctly cleared. If a disease is rare, many positives can be false.

points.ask: How do I read a number?
What do sensitivity and specificity mean?
Why can a good test still mislead?

stages.title: Diagnostic imaging
stages.hook: X-rays, ultrasound, CT and MRI all show inside the body. Why use different ones for different questions?
explain: X-rays pass through the body; dense tissue such as bone absorbs more and appears white, air appears black. They are quick and good for fractures and some chest problems. CT (computed tomography) uses many X-ray images to build detailed slices. It is fast and good for the head in emergencies, bleeding and the abdomen, but uses a higher radiation dose.

Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves and no ionising radiation. It is good for the heart, abdomen, pregnancy and blood flow, and is safe and portable. MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) uses strong magnets and radio waves, not X-rays. It gives excellent detail of soft tissue such as brain, spinal cord and joints but is slower, loud and unsuitable for some metal implants.

Choose imaging by asking: what question? how urgent? what is the benefit versus the risk (radiation, cost, contrast allergy, pregnancy)? Imaging is a tool, not a replacement for the history and examination; scans can show harmless 'incidental' findings that cause worry.

example.q: A fictional patient arrives after a fall with a deformed, painful forearm. Which first imaging is sensible?
steps: The question is: is a bone broken?
X-ray shows bone well and is quick and available.
So an X-ray of the forearm is the first choice.

analogies.home: A torch shows shadows (X-ray), sonar finds depth (ultrasound), a scanner makes slices (CT).
analogies.sea: A ship uses sonar to see underwater without harming marine life, like ultrasound.
analogies.tech: A 3D scanner builds an object from many slices like CT.
analogies.city: A drone survey, an underground survey and a satellite picture each show a city in different ways.

stages.mnemonic: X-ray bones, CT quick slices, Ultrasound safe and live, MRI soft tissue detail.
terms: An image using ionising radiation, good for bone.
Many X-ray images combined into detailed slices.
Imaging with sound waves, no ionising radiation.
Imaging with magnets and radio waves, excellent for soft tissue.

misc.right: Some scans use radiation and can lead to unnecessary follow-up, so scans should be justified by the clinical question.

stages.limits: Doses and availability differ between hospitals and countries. Choice of test follows local guidelines and radiologists' advice.

stages.title: Infectious diseases
stages.hook: Some infections spread by coughs, others by mosquitoes, others by water. Why does the route of spread matter for control?
explain: Infectious diseases are caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. Spread can be by respiratory droplets or aerosols (influenza, tuberculosis), contact, food and water (cholera, typhoid), insect vectors (malaria, dengue), blood and body fluids, or from mother to baby. The chain of infection runs: agent, reservoir, exit, transmission, entry and a susceptible host. Breaking any link controls spread.

Control measures include hand hygiene, clean water and sanitation, vaccines, masks and ventilation for airborne spread, mosquito nets and vector control, safe food handling, isolation and treatment of cases. The incubation period is the time from infection to symptoms.

Antimicrobials target particular groups: antibiotics for bacteria, antivirals for some viruses, antifungals for fungi, antiparasitic drugs for parasites. Antimicrobial resistance develops when microbes survive drugs, so these medicines should be used only when needed. Sepsis, a dangerous whole-body response to infection, is an emergency: fever or low temperature, fast heart rate and breathing, confusion, low blood pressure.

example.q: A fictional village has a malaria outbreak in the rainy season. Which control step breaks the chain?
steps: Malaria is spread by mosquito bites.
Bed nets and reducing standing water reduce bites and mosquitoes.
Treating cases reduces the parasite reservoir.
example.a: Bed nets, mosquito control and treating cases

analogies.home: A chain breaks if any link is cut. Cutting one link of infection stops spread.
analogies.city: Roads carry traffic; closing a road stops traffic. Blocking routes stops infection.
analogies.farm: Fences and clean water troughs reduce disease between animals.
analogies.sea: Ports use quarantine to stop disease coming off ships.

stages.mnemonic: Agent, Reservoir, Exit, Transmission, Entry, Host: break any link.
terms: A living carrier, such as a mosquito, that passes on an infection.
Time between infection and the first symptoms.
When microbes stop responding to drugs that once killed them.
A life-threatening reaction to infection that can damage organs.

misc.right: Antibiotics only treat bacterial infections. Viruses, fungi and parasites need different treatments.

stages.limits: Disease details vary between regions and outbreaks; treatment decisions follow local guidelines.

trip.prompt: Find an example disease and cut one link in its chain.

questions.q: Mosquitoes spreading malaria are an example of a...
o: Vector
Reservoir only
Vaccine
Antibiotic
questions.why: A vector carries an agent between hosts.

Mosquito nets over the bed
Wearing masks only

o: Time from infection to symptoms

The time taken to recover fully

questions.why: Travel history is a crucial clue.

questions.q: Explain how vaccination reduces the spread of an infection in a community.
questions.model: Vaccinated people are protected and less likely to pass on the germ, so the chain of spread is broken and even unvaccinated people are safer when coverage is high.

o: It removes the source from contact with susceptible people

panel.why: It breaks the chain of transmission.

panel.q: A viral infection is wrongly treated with antibiotics. What are the harms?

A faster cure of the infection

panel.q: Why does knowing the route of spread help choose control measures?
panel.model: Different routes need different barriers, such as clean water for waterborne disease, ventilation for airborne disease and nets for mosquito-borne disease, so we target the link that is actually used.

teach.topic: How infections spread and are stopped
teach.model: Infections spread through a chain: germ, source, exit, route, entry and a susceptible person. Cutting any link stops spread, for example by clean water, vaccines, nets or masks. Antibiotics only work on bacteria.

stages.title: Emergency medicine and triage
stages.hook: Ten patients arrive at once and there are only three beds. Who is seen first, and who decides?
explain: Triage means sorting patients by urgency so the sickest are treated first, not by who arrived first. Systems use colours or numbers: for example immediate (red), urgent (yellow), delayed (green) and expectant or dead (black) in major incidents. Triage is repeated because patients can get better or worse.

The ABCDE approach checks the most life-threatening problems in order: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability (consciousness, glucose) and Exposure (full examination, temperature). Treat each problem as you find it, and call for help early. Simple tools such as the early warning score flag patients who are getting worse.

Red flags needing immediate help include a blocked or noisy airway, severe breathing difficulty, signs of shock (cold clammy skin, fast pulse, low blood pressure), unresponsiveness, seizures that will not stop, chest pain with sweating, and signs of stroke. A junior's job is to recognise the emergency, start simple safe steps, call for help and communicate clearly (for example with SBAR: situation, background, assessment, recommendation).

example.q: Three fictional patients arrive: a child with a small graze, an adult with chest pain and sweating, and a teen with a sprained ankle. Who is seen first?
steps: Chest pain with sweating is a possible heart attack: life-threatening.
A sprain is painful but not life-threatening.
A graze is minor. Order: chest pain, then ankle, then graze (reassessing all).
example.a: The adult with chest pain and sweating

analogies.city: Fire crews go to the building with people inside first.
analogies.sea: A lifeboat rescues those in the water before those on deck.
analogies.sport: A medic runs first to the player who is not moving.
analogies.home: If two things go wrong, deal with the fire before the dripping tap.

stages.mnemonic: ABCDE: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure. SBAR for the call.
terms: Sorting patients by how urgently they need care.
A step-by-step check of life-threatening problems.
Inadequate blood flow to the organs, often with low blood pressure.
A way to give clear urgent information: situation, background, assessment, recommendation.

misc.wrong: Patients are seen in the order they arrive.
misc.right: In an emergency department, the sickest are seen first, and waiting patients are reassessed.

stages.limits: Triage tools and colour codes differ between countries and hospitals; resources change what is possible.

stages.title: Clinical ethics and patient safety
stages.hook: A patient refuses a treatment you believe would help. Whose decision is it, and what must you do?
explain: Four widely used principles of medical ethics are autonomy (respect for the patient's choices), beneficence (do good), non-maleficence (do no harm) and justice (fairness in who gets care). They sometimes conflict, so clinicians weigh them and discuss with colleagues.

Consent must be informed, voluntary and given by someone with capacity, meaning they can understand, retain, weigh and communicate a decision. A capable adult may refuse treatment even when clinicians disagree. When capacity is lacking, decisions follow the law and the patient's best interests, involving family and the care team. Confidentiality means information is shared only with those who need it, with limited exceptions such as serious risk to others, set by law.

Patient safety means preventing avoidable harm. Most errors come from systems, not bad people, so hospitals use checklists, double checks, clear handovers, open reporting and a just culture. When something goes wrong, be honest with the patient (duty of candour), report it and learn. Patients should be treated fairly regardless of background.

example.q: A fictional adult with capacity declines a recommended treatment. What should the team do?
steps: Check capacity: can the patient understand, retain, weigh and communicate?
Explain the risks, benefits and alternatives clearly and check understanding.
If capable, respect the decision, keep the door open and document it.
example.a: Respect the informed choice of a capable adult, keep talking and document

analogies.home: A family decides together but each person chooses for themself where they can.
analogies.sport: A referee applies the same rules to both teams, like justice.
analogies.tech: Good software has safeguards so one slip does not crash everything.
analogies.sea: A ship's crew uses checklists and lookouts because even good sailors make errors.

terms: The right of a capable person to make their own decisions.
The ability to understand, retain, weigh and communicate a decision.
An error caught before it harms the patient.

misc.wrong: Medical errors only happen because of careless people.
misc.right: Most errors arise from system weaknesses such as fatigue, poor handover or confusing labels; fixing systems prevents repeat harm.

stages.limits: Laws on consent, confidentiality, age of decision-making and end-of-life care differ between countries and cultures, and reasonable people disagree on hard cases.

panel.q: Why is it better to fix systems than only blame the person after an error?

teach.model: Doctors respect patients' choices, try to do good, avoid harm and be fair. Consent must be informed and voluntary. Most errors come from weak systems, so we report them honestly and learn.

points.ask: What do we do about mistakes?
